Case Vignette: Amir

Amir is a 48-year-old fashion designer, a man whose hands move with a precision that seems almost separate from the rest of him. He presents as meticulously dressed, but there is a weariness in his eyes that no bespoke suit can hide. He speaks with a careful, deliberate cadence, as if he is constantly editing his own thoughts.

The story he tells begins in a different life, in his hometown of Beirut, two years ago. He was at the peak of his career, having just finished a successful show during Beirut Fashion Week. The city was electric, and he felt a profound sense of belonging, a connection to the vibrant, chaotic pulse of his heritage. The afternoon of August 4, 2020, started like any other. He was in his atelier, a converted warehouse overlooking the port, pinning a silk gown on a mannequin. He remembers the sunlight falling on the fabric, the hum of the sewing machine.

Then, the world ended. Not figuratively. The first explosion was a low, chest-rattling thud that he felt in his molars. He thought of a gas canister. Then, the second one. It was a wall of sound and light that erased everything. He has no memory of the blast wave itself, only the aftermath. He came to on the floor, his ears ringing with a high-pitched, electronic shriek, the world a monochrome of grey dust. The mannequin was gone. The wall was gone. He could see the sky where the port had been, a vast, roiling cloud of ochre and black. A woman’s shoe lay near his hand, still on its heel.

He walked for hours, he thinks. He found his sister’s apartment, her face a mask of blood from a cut on her forehead. He helped her, his hands shaking, his mind a blank white sheet. He stayed in Beirut for three months, but the city had become a phantom limb. Every car backfire, every slamming door, every sudden shout on the street sent a jolt of pure, animal terror through him. He stopped driving, his heart hammering at the sight of a yellow truck. He couldn’t work. The silk felt like sandpaper. The colors of his fabrics seemed to bleed into each other.

He came to London eight months ago, seeking a quiet that he cannot find. He lives alone in a minimalist flat in Clerkenwell. He has a small, high-end clientele, but his work has changed. He used to design for opulence, for drama, for the joy of a silhouette. Now, he designs for armor. His collections are structured, severe, with high collars and stiff, protective fabrics. He calls it "architectural," but he knows it is a fortress.

He cannot sleep. Not really. He falls into a shallow, fitful rest around 4 a.m., only to be woken by a recurring dream: he is in his atelier, but the mannequin is a woman, and she is silently screaming, her mouth a black hole. He jolts awake, his heart a frantic drum, his body soaked in a cold sweat. The sound of a lorry braking outside his window can send him to the floor, hands over his head, for twenty minutes.

He has no friends here. He tried a dinner party, but the sound of a champagne cork popping sent him reeling into the bathroom, where he stared at his own hollow face in the mirror, unable to breathe. He has been divorced for five years, and the distance from his ex-wife, who still lives in Beirut, is a relief. He cannot bear her grief, layered on top of his own. He feels a profound, unshakeable guilt. He survived. He walked away. He carries the weight of those who did not, a heavy, invisible garment he cannot take off. He is not a designer anymore. He is a man holding his breath, waiting for the next explosion.
